slides.title: Real-World Scale Drawings
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: a scale with two units is a rate — read it per 1 unit, then multiply or divide.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the move Notes I makes on a scale: per 1 unit first. A room that cannot write 90 for 2 as 45 for 1 will not write ¼ in : 1 ft as 1 in : 4 ft. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the scale and its rewrite.
slides.note: ¼ in : 1 ft says a quarter inch of paper stands for a foot of room. Multiply both sides by 4: 1 in : 4 ft — every inch on the paper is 4 feet in the room. Now it is the warm-up's unit rate, and every question is a multiplication or a division by 4. **Say:** rewrite the scale per 1 unit of drawing before you touch a question.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: A room 2 in by 2.5 in at 1 in : 4 ft is 8 ft by 10 ft, so 80 ft². The drawing's area is 5 in², and 5 × 4 = 20 is wrong — yesterday's lesson: area is two lengths, so the rate is used twice (5 × 16 = 80). The safe route is the real dimensions first. **Say:** find the real length and the real width, then multiply.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: A 14-ft wall at 1 in : 4 ft: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5 in on the paper. The real length is bigger, so the drawing length is smaller — the division makes it smaller, and an estimate (14 ft is a little more than 3 inches' worth) says so. **Say:** from the room to the paper, divide by the rate.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: A room's real dimensions and area.
slides.note: Ask for the scale per 1 inch before anyone multiplies.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 1 in : 4 ft; 10 ft by 12 ft; 120 ft². A board with 30 scaled the drawing's area (7.5 in²) by 4 — the named error.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 6 by 16; 96 ft². A board with 24 scaled 6 in² by 4.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: The scale is not printed: make it from one pair.
slides.note: Ask what the scale is before anyone touches the 6 — nobody multiplies until it is written per 1 inch.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: The pair gives the scale: 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5 ft per inch. Then 6 × 4.5 = 27 ft. A board with 20 added 2 ft for 2 more inches — the additive error; one with 9 doubled 4.5 instead of multiplying by 6.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 6.5 ft per inch; 32.5 ft. A board with 16 added.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.note: Diagnostic. A 1 : 50 scale has one unit: 1 cm of model is 50 cm of car. C is right until the unit; a 400-m car is a sanity check that a room full of C skipped. Sixty seconds and a re-vote on a split.

slides.note: The boundary board: area is asked, and the room has to go to real units first. A is yesterday's error in today's clothes — 6 × 4 uses the rate once, and area needs it twice. On a split, draw the 8 by 12 room.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
